title: The supplement industry isn't selling efficacy, it's selling relief from uncertainty
dek: The world spends $6 billion a year on menopause supplements while the UK spent only £60 million researching menopause that same year; collagen goes from slaughterhouse waste at £15 a kilo to a £300 beauty product on the shelf.
why: Medium information density, but three things are worth the price: the cost accounting on collagen, the billion-dollar failed vitamin D trials, and the funding gap in menopause research. The novel discussion in the back half can be skipped.
who: Anyone who has bought collagen, a multivitamin, or a private health check, plus founders and investors in health consumer goods and supplement brands — the first half has hard material on cost structure and evidence quality.
skip: From 30:05, the discussion of the characters in the novel Country People and the hollow earth has nothing to do with health consumerism.

points.body: Zand van Tulleken gives the mechanism straight: collagen is the waste of meat and fishing processing — fish heads, fish bones, oxtail, cow ears, cow hooves, all of it otherwise destined for disposal. Ground up, boiled in hydrochloric acid, and turned into a beauty product, the wholesale price goes from £15 a kilo to £300 a kilo on the high street, a markup he describes as the kind you get selling cocaine. So his conclusion is not "collagen doesn't work" but: even if you believe it works, you are being fleeced — boiling chicken bones yourself gets you the same thing.

points.h: Remove the industry-funded studies and the effect disappears
points.body: There are two ways to read whether collagen works. Pool all the studies and the conclusion is that it helps joint pain, skin appearance and elasticity; remove the industry-funded studies and the effect disappears. Zand says that in itself should be a very large clue. The methodology applies beyond collagen — when he gets to multivitamins he stresses that even if you believe the pill in the bottle works, "what's actually in the bottle" is a separate question, and adulteration, contamination and damage to the scientific literature are harms independent of efficacy.

points.h: The billion-dollar failed vitamin D trials
points.body: When Zand was in medical school, every doctor believed vitamin D had those exciting effects on the heart and the brain, and a mass of research suggested as much. But when vitamin D was tested as a drug, roughly a billion dollars was spent over the past decade, by people who badly wanted to find those benefits, and nothing was found. The NHS now advises considering a low-dose supplement, especially in winter, which is good advice; but high doses may be harmful, and it won't give you the sparkle you were expecting. He adds that many people who did what was then widely accepted shouldn't feel like fools — the evidence has changed a great deal in just a few years.

points.h: Menopause: $6 billion on supplements, $60 million on research
points.body: Zand says the menopause chapter was the hardest to write, because in the other chapters he is a victim alongside the reader, whereas in this one "nothing is coming for me": the medical profession lets you down first, and then you are pushed into the arms of the wellness industry, in a very insidious way. He gives the numbers: the world spends $6 billion a year on menopause supplements, while the UK spent only about $60 million on menopause research last year — the UK doesn't even record how much is spent on menopause research, because the sum is too small. His judgment: the industry is selling doubt and hope, and the first emotion people want to resolve is "I don't want to have this problem," and the second is hope.

points.h: The brain rewards the question, not the answer
points.body: The neuroscience Lani Watson cites is counterintuitive: when a question sparks curiosity, reward circuits connected to the hippocampus light up and the brain enters a state of "ready to learn," after which incoming information is easier to encode and easier to recall — and it doesn't have to be the answer to that particular question, because the brain doesn't distinguish in that state. More importantly, the research shows we don't get the same reward when we find the answer. In other words, the brain rewards asking and staying in curiosity, not digging the answer out.

points.h: Socrates would go after the wellness gurus
points.body: Lani holds Socrates up as the model for a 21st-century questioning mindset: he deliberately sought out people who claimed certainty and dragged them into a state called aporia — confusion, blankness, uncertainty. She says Socrates would have adored the wellness gurus, and would walk into the city square (today, the digital square) and ask them: how can you be certain what health is? What wellness is? What a vitamin is? She concedes Socrates had flaws, was famously annoying, and was ultimately put to death for being an annoying questioner and for challenging authority and the status quo.

points.h: 400 biomarkers are answers to questions you never asked
points.body: Zand contrasts two paths in medicine: he was trained the old way, which emphasizes asking questions and letting the patient tell their story; now you can go to a private company and buy a panel of 400 biomarkers. His line is that it's a pile of "answers to questions you never asked" — they put up a poster asking "is something off with you?", ask the question, then hand you the answer directly, and you play almost no role beyond paying and handing over your data. And among 400 blood chemistry answers, some will be wrong, and will take you somewhere very bad. That is also why the industry is hard to regulate: doctors use the same blood tests, but doctors are answering very specific questions.

points.h: The hollow earth belief is actually moving
points.body: Daniel Mason first put the hollow earth in his novel because it was comic, a step "worse" than flat earth, a way to push our beliefs about the world one step further. But after reading the sources he changed his mind: the belief is in some way moving, because it shows that at a basic level we want to believe a better place exists — the hollow earth fantasy always contains an untouched kingdom where people are treated more justly, and are more beautiful. In New England especially: as wildlife and forests vanished, people wanted to believe the extinct animals were actually alive underground, a place where vanished creatures could be found. He says he genuinely wishes the hollow earth existed.
